name: Sara Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This interview is confidential. What does an ordinary day at the contact centre look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, have a two-year college diploma, and lead the small team that fixes delivery and payment complaints. I am among the quickest at finding where a parcel trail and a refund trail split. I use the centre’s AI summary now and then, after another agent has checked it, but I read the original chat before approving money back. My pay is low for this work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is waiting when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Matteo and I have two children in school and a mortgage. He stacks shelves on variable shifts, and we have about two weeks of expenses saved. Few similar jobs are close enough for an easy switch. I try not to bring a customer’s anger home, but a missing refund can stay in my head all evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau sounds like the summaries we already use for the easy chats. I would still pin the original delivery scan to each refund correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the job stays, and my team can keep finding the odd mistakes. But two weeks of savings and Matteo’s changing shifts make ordinary bills tight even here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading refunds and use the AI summary only after checking the original customer chat. In the first year of minor change, I’d set aside the small cash-back payment from our grocery card each month for the mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our money, fairly calm about this tool. The parcel can be marked delivered while the customer is still looking at an empty doorstep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What detail does the summary miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the courier scan time with the customer’s address note. Last month a driver used the next building’s entrance, and the summary left that detail out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why that small saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would move the cash-back amount as soon as it lands. It is small, but leaving it in the spending account makes it vanish.

say: I’d say **easy chat summaries** still need the original delivery scan.
I’d show colleagues the **refund record** before closing a claim.
think: I think my **team keeps work** in a mild change.
I worry **two weeks saved** and Matteo’s shifting hours leave little room.
do: Keep **leading refunds** and checking original chats before occasional AI summaries.
Save the **monthly grocery cash-back** for mortgage bills in the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about bills, calm about the small tool change.

steps.text: Keep leading refund corrections and check original chats before using AI summaries
Save monthly grocery cash-back for mortgage payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell agents Steady Disruption could clear the simple chat queue and leave fewer paid people for disputed refunds. I would join a team request for written paid hours and a customer route to challenge a wrong automated refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my skill might keep me on the difficult cases, but the centre could need fewer people to do them. I cannot treat a fast answer as secure hours when Matteo’s warehouse rota is uneven too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d help my team send the paid-hours and refund-appeal demand, then test ten old disputed deliveries with the approved AI system on a paid shift. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid returns role only if written weekly wage and hours cover our mortgage; I would keep this desk until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I want to see the error count before I condemn the tool. A fast refund that goes to the wrong account is a second complaint waiting to happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your test measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its answer with the actual payment ledger, not with another generated summary. If three of ten are wrong, I would show the errors to my team and manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the full week of hours in the posting. A higher hourly rate with half the shifts would not pay the mortgage.

say: I’d seek **written paid hours** with teammates as simple chats move.
I’d demand a **refund appeal route** for customers.
think: I think my **hard-case skill** may keep some work.
I fear **fewer paid agents** and Matteo’s variable hours together.
do: Join the **team hours-and-appeals demand** and test ten old delivery disputes with AI on paid time in 2026.
Apply for **posted returns work** only with written mortgage-covering weekly wage and hours; stay until signed offer.
feel: **Anxious**, yet willing to check real errors.

fieldNote: She tests **actual ledgers** rather than generated summaries.

steps.text: Join teammates demanding written paid hours and refund appeal rights

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 could settle a refund without anyone reading the customer’s evidence. I would join colleagues in demanding written rota notice and a way to reopen a wrong machine decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my team’s paid hours could vanish quickly in 2028 even though we handle the hard cases. Robots around 2031 are beside the point for a screen and headset job, and two weeks saved buys almost no search time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d help send that group demand and postpone the planned garden fence while the old one is safe. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid claims role only with written mortgage-covering weekly wage and hours, keeping my present job until a signed offer; I’d take a required claims course only if funded on paid time for that vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed; the household cannot absorb a missed pay packet. Two weeks of savings is shorter than most hiring processes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the fence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Matteo (my husband) the fence can stand another season if it stays safe. We would keep the money for the mortgage and the children’s travel to school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make training possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a real posting and the training hours on my paid rota. I cannot pay a fee for the possibility of work.

say: I’d warn **2028 AGI** may close refunds without reading customer evidence.
I’d demand **rota notice and appeals** with colleagues.
think: I think my **team hours** could disappear in 2028.
I know **two weeks saved** cannot cover a long search.
do: Join the **group rota-and-appeals demand** and postpone the safe fence in 2026.
Apply for **posted claims work** after 2028 with written mortgage-covering weekly pay and hours; stay until signed offer.
Take a **required claims course** only if funded on paid time for that posted paid vacancy.
S2.quote: Two weeks of savings is shorter than most hiring processes.
fieldNote: The **2028 deadline** reaches her refund work before 2031 robots.
The **safe fence delay** protects mortgage cash.
A course requires a **real vacancy** and paid funded time.

steps.text: Join colleagues demanding written rota notice and reopened automated refund appeals
Postpone garden fence while old fence remains safe
Apply for posted claims work after 2028 with written mortgage-covering pay/hours; stay until signed offer
Take required funded claims course on paid time only for posted paid vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us time to make the centre write down which jobs remain paid. I would ask colleagues to demand funded paid-time claims training only for posted openings, not a vague promise to upskill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can learn claims review if there is a real job at the end, but full AGI may take that work too. Five years gives us more evenings to compare terms, not enough spare money for an unpaid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d join that staff demand and take a funded claims-review course on paid time only if a posted paid vacancy requires it. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for the posted role only with written mortgage-covering weekly wage and hours and stay in my current job until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with room to test a route instead of guessing. A course is useful only when I can point to the paid chair it leads to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise in class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to trace a missing payment from the bank receipt into the centre ledger during class. If the lesson is only a slide deck, it will not prepare me for a disputed bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What cost might change the decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the weekly wage next to our mortgage and the cost of getting to that office. The move has to work after travel, not just on the advertisement.

say: I’d seek **posted paid roles** before anyone enrolls in training.
I’d demand **funded paid-time study** with colleagues for required courses.
think: I think I could learn **claims review** for a real opening.
I doubt a **new certificate** alone protects work from AGI.
do: Join the **staff training demand** and take required funded claims training on paid time for a posted paid vacancy.
Apply for **posted claims work** after 2031 only with written mortgage-covering weekly wage and hours after travel; stay until signed offer.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to check a real route.
S3.quote: A course is useful only when I can point to the paid chair it leads to.
fieldNote: She wants **payment-ledger practice** rather than a slide deck in the required course.
The **posted paid vacancy** and funded study hours are gates for training.
She subtracts **travel costs** before comparing weekly pay with the mortgage.

steps.text: Join staff demand for funded paid-time claims training tied to posted paid openings
Take required funded claims course on paid time only for posted paid vacancy
Apply for posted claims role after 2031 with written mortgage-covering net pay/hours; stay until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 leaves time to inspect every new refund system before the centre cuts paid appeal hours. I would keep joining colleagues’ yearly demand for the appeal rota and error figures in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can earn and save while my team still corrects refunds, but full thinking AI could take that desk in 2036. Robots around 2039 do not make the headset safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the refund desk, save a fixed part of each payday and join the annual group demand for paid appeal hours. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for a posted paid claims job only if my hours fall and its written weekly wage and hours cover the mortgage after travel, keeping my current job until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far horizon and anxious about the next school bill. A decade is enough to build a buffer only if we can keep earning through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the team compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have the team compare reopened refunds with the paid appeal hours on each rota. If errors rise while appeal hours fall, we can show what the savings cost customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would saving work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set the savings transfer for payday, before small purchases eat it. Matteo’s warehouse shifts change, so I cannot promise the same amount from his wage.

say: I’d seek **written appeal hours** and error figures with colleagues each year.
I’d insist on **checking new systems** before paid appeal shifts shrink.
think: I think I can **earn and save** while refund corrections remain.
I know **2036 thinking AI** could still take my desk.
do: Keep the **refund desk**, save part of each payday and join annual group demands for paid appeal hours.
Apply for **posted claims work** after 2036 if hours fall, with written mortgage-covering pay and hours after travel; stay until signed offer.
feel: **Uneasy** about 2036, anxious about current school bills.
S4.quote: A decade is enough to build a buffer only if we can keep earning through it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the first cut could be the paid hours of my whole small team. I would need written rota notice, a real paid vacancy with weekly pay and hours that clear our mortgage, and funded training on paid time if the vacancy requires it. A group agreement on reviewing wrong refunds would help customers too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a faster reply gets the missing refund back. A customer cannot pay a bill with an apology sent in three seconds.

headlineQuote: A customer cannot pay a bill with an apology sent in three seconds.
portrait: At **43**, Sara leads difficult refund work after a two-year college diploma but earns low pay.
She and Matteo support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with about two weeks saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** after checking the original chat.
She weighs **paid hours** and refund corrections before accepting new systems.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut the paid hours of her small team quickly.
whatWouldHelp: **Written rota notice**, mortgage-covering posted work, required funded paid-time training and shared refund review terms would help.
